passages.t: In the beginning was the Word
passages.happening:
John opens his book before the world began. “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (verse 1). The Word was there at the very start. Everything that exists was made through him: “without Him nothing was made that has been made” (verse 3).

In him was life, and that life was light for people. The light still shines in the dark, and the dark has not put it out (verse 5).

John does not yet say who the Word is. He will, in verse 14. For now he lets the reader stand at the edge of creation and listen.
passages.hearers:
Jewish hearers knew this opening at once. The Bible's first line is “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1). And in Genesis God makes the world by speaking: ‘And God said, Let there be light’. To a Jewish hearer, God's word was God himself acting. A psalm says, “By the word of the LORD the heavens were made” (Psalm 33:6). They also knew the picture of God's Wisdom beside him at creation, like a master builder (Proverbs 8:22-31).

Greek hearers knew the word too. Logos, the Greek word behind ‘Word’, also means ‘reason’ or ‘account’. Some Greek thinkers, Heraclitus long before and the Stoics after him, used logos for the reason that holds the whole universe in order.

So John chose a word both kinds of hearer would know. Then, in verse 14, he says what neither of them expected: this Word became a man.
passages.ot: These verses echo Genesis 1 on purpose. The same opening words, “In the beginning” (Genesis 1:1). A world made by God's word. Light shining into darkness on the first day (Genesis 1:3-5). John is telling his readers that the story of Jesus starts where the Bible starts. It is a story of new creation.
passages.hard:
Does ‘the Word was God’ mean the Word is God, or ‘a god’? The New World Translation, the Bible used by Jehovah's Witnesses, ends verse 1 with ‘the Word was a god’. Its reason is a point of Greek grammar. In this clause the Greek word for God has no ‘the’ in front of it. Greek has no word for ‘a’, so translators have to decide.

Most Greek scholars, of many churches and of none, answer this way. In Greek, a describing word placed before the verb often has no ‘the’, even when it is definite; E. C. Colwell showed this in 1933. And such a word usually tells you what kind of thing the subject is; Philip Harner argued this in the Journal of Biblical Literature in 1973. So the clause means: what God is, the Word is. The Word shares God's own nature. It does not say the Word is the Father. The line before has just said that the Word was ‘with God’.

Notice too that in this same chapter John writes ‘God’ with no ‘the’ in verses 6, 12, 13 and 18, and each time he means the one true God. No one translates those ‘a god’. And John's faith was Israel's faith: there is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4). A second, lesser god beside him would break that faith, not keep it.

Christians who read ‘the Word was God’ are not saying there are two Gods. They confess that the Father and the Son are distinct, and are one God. People who read the verse differently are sincere and deserve a patient answer, not scorn. The answer is in the Greek, and in the rest of the book. At its end Thomas will say to the risen Jesus, “My Lord and my God” (20:28).
passages.asks: John begins with God, not with us. Before we ask what Jesus can do for us, John asks us to see who he is: the one through whom everything was made, you included. If he made all things, nothing in your life is outside his reach. And if the dark has not put out his light, no darkness you face has the last word.

passages.t: A witness, and a light refused and received
passages.happening:
Now a man steps into the story: “There came a man who was sent from God. His name was John” (verse 6). This is John the Baptist, not the writer of the book. He came as a witness, to point people to the light. He was not the light himself (verse 8).

The true light was coming into the world. But the world he made did not know him (verse 10). “He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him” (verse 11). Yet some did. To all who received him, to those who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God. They were born, not because of their family line or because someone wanted them, but of God (verses 12-13).
passages.hearers:
A witness, in the ancient world as now, was someone who told a court what he had seen. John's Gospel is full of court words: testify, testimony, witness, judge. From its first page the book reads like a trial about who Jesus is, with witnesses called one by one.

Why does John stress that the Baptist ‘was not the Light’? Because the Baptist was famous. The Jewish historian Josephus, writing near the end of the first century, calls him a good man who urged people to live justly and to come to baptism (Antiquities 18.116-119). Years later, in Ephesus, Paul met disciples who knew only John's baptism (Acts 19:1-7). Some people honoured John very highly. This Gospel gives him every honour as a witness, and no more.

‘His own’ in verse 11 means first his own world, which he made, and his own people, Israel. But the refusal is not only theirs. Verse 10 says ‘the world’ did not know him. The whole human race is in view.
passages.ot: ‘Children of God’ was Israel's name before it was anyone else's. God called Israel “My firstborn son” (Exodus 4:22), and Moses told the people, “You are sons of the LORD your God” (Deuteronomy 14:1). John says this family is now entered by a new birth from God (verse 13). Jesus will explain that birth to Nicodemus in chapter 3.
passages.hard: Does verse 13 mean that people have no part in becoming God's children? Verse 12 says they ‘received’ him and ‘believed in His name’. Verse 13 says they were born ‘not of blood, nor of the desire or will of man, but born of God’. Christians have long discussed how these fit. Some stress that God acts first; some stress the human answer. Both halves are in the text, side by side. No one becomes God's child by family line or by effort. And no one becomes God's child without receiving him.
passages.asks: Your birth family does not decide your place in God's family. Some readers come from families that loved them well, and some from families that let them down. Either way the door is the same: receiving the light and trusting his name. Where have you been waiting to be good enough, or from the right family, to be let in?

passages.happening:
Now John says it plainly. “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (verse 14). The Word, who was God, became a real human being, with a body that could be tired, hungry and hurt. And the people around him saw his glory, ‘full of grace and truth’.

John the Baptist cries out that the one who comes after him is greater, because he was before him (verse 15). From his fullness, the writer says, we have all received ‘grace upon grace’ (verse 16). The law came through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (verse 17). No one has ever seen God. But the one and only Son, who is himself God and is at the Father's side, has made him known (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
‘Flesh’ was a strong word. It meant human nature at its weakest: frail, mortal, able to bleed. John's word leaves no room to say that the Son of God only seemed to be human.

‘Made His dwelling’ is, in Greek, ‘pitched his tent’. A Jewish hearer would think of the tabernacle, the tent in the wilderness where God met his people: “the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle” (Exodus 40:34). Now God's glory lives in a person.

‘Full of grace and truth’ would ring a bell too. When Moses asked to see God's glory, God passed by and called himself “abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). Many readers hear John's ‘grace and truth’ as an echo of that pair.

Verse 18 holds a small question about the old copies. The oldest copies, the papyri P66 and P75 and the great fourth-century books, read ‘the one and only God’ here; many later copies read ‘the only begotten Son’. Most modern Bibles follow the older copies, as the Berean Standard Bible does: ‘the one and only Son, who is Himself God’.
passages.ot: Verse 17 sets Moses beside Jesus. This is not an attack on the law. The law was God's gift through Moses. But when Moses asked to see God's glory, God said, “You cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live” (Exodus 33:20). John says that what Moses could not see has now been made known, in a face. The tent where the glory came down (Exodus 40:34-35) and the glory Moses glimpsed from a rock (Exodus 33:18-23) both point to this.
passages.hard: If ‘no one has ever seen God’ (verse 18), what did Isaiah see in the temple (Isaiah 6:1), or Moses and the elders on the mountain (Exodus 24:9-11)? Readers have answered in two ways. Some say those were visions and glimpses, not God as he is in himself. Others say that whenever God was seen in the Old Testament, it was the Son who made him known. Either way, John's point holds: the fullest showing of God is Jesus himself.
passages.asks: We often want God to prove himself from a distance: a sign in the sky, a voice. John's answer is a person you can come close to. If you want to know what God is like, look at Jesus: how he treats the outsider, the grieving, the guilty. Is the God you picture as full of grace and truth as the one John saw?

passages.t: Not the Christ, but a voice
passages.happening:
Leaders in Jerusalem send priests and Levites to ask John the Baptist, “Who are you?” (verse 19). He says plainly, “I am not the Christ” (verse 20). Are you Elijah? ‘I am not.’ Are you the Prophet? ‘No.’ Then who are you? John answers with words from Isaiah: “I am a voice of one calling in the wilderness, ‘Make straight the way for the Lord’” (verse 23).

Some Pharisees in the group then ask why he baptizes at all. John says he baptizes with water, but someone is standing among them whom they do not know. John is not worthy even to untie that man's sandal straps (verses 26-27). All this happens at Bethany beyond the Jordan (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
John says that ‘the Jews of Jerusalem’ sent these men (verse 19). Here, as often in this Gospel, the phrase means the authorities in Jerusalem, not the Jewish people as a whole. John the Baptist, the priests and the Levites are all Jews.

Jewish hope at this time had more than one shape, and the questions show three. ‘The Christ’ is the Greek form of ‘Messiah’: the anointed king from David's family. ‘Elijah’: the prophet Elijah had been taken up into heaven alive (2 Kings 2:11), and Malachi said God would send him back before the great day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5). ‘The Prophet’: Moses had promised that God would raise up a prophet like him (Deuteronomy 18:15). John says no to all three, and calls himself only a voice: a sound that points, and then fades.

The sandal saying would land hard. Untying a master's sandals was a slave's job. A later Jewish saying, in the Talmud and credited to a rabbi of the third century, says that a student should do for his teacher everything a slave does for his master, except take off his shoes (Ketubbot 96a). If people already thought that way in John's day, the Baptist is saying he is not fit to do even the job a student was spared.

Bethany beyond the Jordan is not the Bethany near Jerusalem where Lazarus lived. Its site is not certain. A place on the east bank of the river, Al-Maghtas, was listed as a World Heritage Site in 2015 under the name ‘Bethany beyond the Jordan’, but there is no firm proof that this is the spot.
passages.ot: John answers in the words of Isaiah 40:3. In Isaiah the voice calls for a road through the desert, because God himself is coming back to his people after their exile. So the Baptist is saying more than ‘I am humble’. He is saying that the Lord is about to arrive. Another Jewish group of that time, whose writings were found at Qumran near the Dead Sea, also took Isaiah 40:3 as their calling. Their Community Rule links preparing the way in the wilderness with the study of the law of Moses.
passages.hard: In Matthew, Jesus says of John, “he is the Elijah who was to come” (Matthew 11:14). Here John says, ‘I am not’ (verse 21). Is that a contradiction? Many readers answer that John denies being Elijah come back in person, the man taken up into heaven, while Jesus speaks of John's role. Luke says John would go before the Lord “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17). Others think the Gospels remember John from different angles. Careful readers hold both answers.
passages.asks: John had a crowd, and he could have kept it. Instead he said ‘I am not’ three times, and pointed away from himself. Where are you tempted to take the credit, or the place, that belongs to someone else, or to Christ? Being a voice that points is not a small calling.

passages.happening:
The next day John sees Jesus coming toward him and says, “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (verse 29). This is the one he spoke of, he says, the one who was before him.

Then John tells what he saw. The Spirit came down from heaven like a dove and rested on Jesus (verse 32). God had told John that the one on whom the Spirit comes down and rests is the one who will baptize with the Holy Spirit. So John says, “I have seen and testified that this is the Son of God” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
To a Jewish hearer a lamb meant sacrifice, and more than one kind. Every spring, at Passover, each household killed a lamb, remembering the lamb whose blood saved Israel in Egypt (Exodus 12:3-13). Every day at the temple one lamb was offered in the morning and another in the evening (Exodus 29:38-42). And Isaiah had spoken of God's servant who carried the sins of many and was ‘led like a lamb to the slaughter’ (Isaiah 53:7).

‘The sin of the world’ is wide. Not only Israel's sins. Not a list of sins, but the sin of the whole world, as one load to be carried away.

What John stresses about the Spirit is that it ‘rests’ and remains on Jesus. The prophets had promised this of the coming king from Jesse's family, David's father: “The Spirit of the LORD will rest on Him” (Isaiah 11:2).
passages.ot: Which lamb did John mean? Readers give several answers, and they need not cancel each other. The Passover lamb: this Gospel ends with Jesus dying on the day of Preparation, with none of his bones broken, as the law said of the Passover lamb (19:36; Exodus 12:46). The servant of Isaiah 53, silent ‘like a lamb’ and carrying sin. The lambs of the daily offering. Some also think of Abraham's words to Isaac: “God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering” (Genesis 22:8). And some scholars think the Baptist pictured a strong lamb, a leader who wins the victory, like the Lamb in Revelation who will ‘triumph over them’ (Revelation 17:14). The writer seems glad to let the title carry all of these.
passages.asks: John did not point to Jesus first as an example to copy. He pointed to him as the one who carries sin away. What are you still trying to carry yourself? John spoke of the sin of ‘the world’. That takes in you, and the person you find hardest to forgive.

passages.happening:
The next day John is standing with two of his disciples. He sees Jesus walk by and says again, “Look, the Lamb of God” (verse 36). The two follow Jesus. Jesus turns and asks them, “What do you want?” (verse 38). They call him Rabbi and ask where he is staying. “Come and see,” he says (verse 39). They go, and spend the rest of the day with him. It is about the tenth hour.

One of the two is Andrew. The first thing he does is find his brother Simon and tell him, “We have found the Messiah” (verse 41). He brings Simon to Jesus. Jesus looks at him and gives him a new name: Cephas, which means Peter (verse 42).
passages.hearers:
Disciples in that world followed a teacher on the road and lived near him, to learn a way of life, not just ideas. ‘Rabbi’ was a word of respect for a teacher, and John translates it for readers who did not know Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in the land (verse 38).

The ‘tenth hour’, counting from sunrise, was about four in the afternoon, late enough that they probably stayed the night.

‘Cephas’ is the Aramaic word for rock; ‘Peter’ is the Greek. A new name in Scripture often marks a new calling: Abram became Abraham (Genesis 17:5), and Jacob became Israel (Genesis 32:28). Jesus names Simon for what he will make of him, not for what he already is. On the night of the arrest Peter will be anything but a rock (18:15-27).
passages.ot: Andrew's words carry Israel's long hope. ‘Messiah’ is Hebrew for ‘anointed one’. Israel's kings were anointed with oil when they were chosen; Samuel anointed David “in the presence of his brothers” (1 Samuel 16:13). The psalms and the prophets looked for an anointed king from David's line who would rule in justice (Psalm 2:2; Isaiah 11:1-5). John translates the word for his readers: ‘Christ’ is the Greek for the same thing.
passages.hard: Who was the second disciple? John names Andrew but not the other. Many readers have wondered whether he is the beloved disciple, who stands behind this book and is never named in it. The text does not say. It leaves him unnamed, as if the writer is content for the reader to stand in that empty place.
passages.asks: Jesus' first words in this Gospel are a question: “What do you want?” It is still the right question to bring to him. Many people come to faith the way Peter did, because someone they knew said, in effect, come and see. Who brought you? And who might you bring, not with an argument, but with an invitation?

passages.happening:
The next day Jesus decides to go to Galilee. He finds Philip and says, ‘Follow me’. Philip is from Bethsaida, the town of Andrew and Peter. Philip finds Nathanael and tells him they have found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about: Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph. Nathanael scoffs, “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” (verse 46). Philip does not argue. ‘Come and see.’

As Nathanael comes near, Jesus says, “Here is a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (verse 47). How do you know me? Nathanael asks. Jesus says he saw him under the fig tree before Philip called him. Nathanael is overwhelmed: “You are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!” (verse 49). Jesus says he will see greater things: “you will all see heaven open and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man” (verse 51).
passages.hearers:
Nazareth was a village in the hills of Galilee, never named in the Old Testament. Nathanael's scorn sounds like the scorn of one small place for the next one over. Jesus does not scold him for it.

‘Under the fig tree’ called up a picture of peace and of time at home. The prophets spoke of a day when everyone would sit under his own vine and fig tree, unafraid (Micah 4:4). John does not say what Nathanael was doing there. The point is that Jesus knew him before they met.

‘A true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit’ may carry a smile. Jacob, the father of Israel, was a man of tricks: he deceived his brother and his father (Genesis 27:35-36). Here is a son of Israel with no trickery in him.
passages.ot: Jesus' promise goes back to Jacob's dream at Bethel. Running from home, Jacob dreamed of a ladder resting on the earth and reaching to heaven, “and God's angels were going up and down the ladder” (Genesis 28:12). He woke and called the place the house of God and the gate of heaven. Jesus says the angels will go up and down ‘on the Son of Man’. He himself is the meeting place of heaven and earth, the true Bethel, which means ‘house of God’. ‘Son of Man’ is the name Jesus most often uses for himself. It recalls the figure in Daniel 7:13-14 who comes to God and is given an everlasting kingdom.
passages.hard: When Nathanael calls Jesus ‘Son of God’, does he already believe Jesus is God? Probably not yet, in the full sense. ‘Son of God’ could be a title for Israel's king; God says to the king in a psalm, “You are My Son” (Psalm 2:7), and Nathanael puts it beside ‘King of Israel’. In the other Gospels the disciples understand slowly. Here they use the right words early, and still have years, and a cross, to learn what the words mean. John's readers already know from verse 1 how much more is true than Nathanael can yet see.
passages.asks: Nathanael came with a prejudice and was met with an invitation, and then with the surprise of being known. Have you written Jesus off because of where he came from, or because of some of the people who speak for him? Philip's answer still stands: come and see. And the one you come to already knows you.
